title: Door Hinge & Screw Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate exactly how many hinges and screws you need for any door. Enter height, weight, and door count — get hinges per door, total screws, and a purchase buffer. Free, instant.
intro: The Door Hinge & Screw Calculator uses the **industry-standard rule of 1 hinge per 30 inches (≈75 cm) of door height**, combined with a **weight-based minimum** (2 for lightweight, 3 for standard, 4 for heavy, 5 for security doors). Each hinge leaf has 2–4 holes, so **screws per hinge = holes per leaf × 2 leaves**. A typical residential door at 80″ (2.05 m) with standard 2-hole hinges needs 3 hinges and 12 screws. The calculator also adds a configurable waste buffer (10–15%) so you never run out mid-job.
keyTakeaway: **Hinges/door = max(weight_minimum, ⌈height_m / 0.75⌉)** · **Screws = hinges × holes_per_leaf × 2**. A standard 2.05 m interior door: 3 hinges + 12 screws + 10% buffer = **14 screws to buy**. A heavy 2.10 m exterior door: 4 hinges + 24 screws.
useCases: New construction: calculating total hinges and screws across 12+ interior doors before placing a bulk order — avoids mid-project hardware runs.
Weekend door replacement: confirming exactly how many screws you need (3 hinges × 4 screws = 12) before heading to the hardware store.
Heavy entry door upgrade: accounting for 4–5 hinges on a 180 lb solid-mahogany exterior door, with 3 holes per leaf for load distribution.
Full house renovation: entering 8 doors at once to get a single consolidated shopping list with waste buffer included.

explanation:
## How It Works

### Core Formula

```
Hinges_per_door  = max(weight_minimum, ⌈height_m / 0.75⌉)
Screws_per_hinge = holes_per_leaf × 2
Total_hinges     = hinges_per_door × number_of_doors
Total_screws     = total_hinges × screws_per_hinge
Buy_screws       = ⌈total_screws × (1 + buffer/100)⌉
```

The **1 hinge per 30 inches (≈75 cm)** rule is the widely-cited industry standard referenced by Hager Companies, Royde & Tucker, VK Hardware, and the National Wood Door Association (NWDA). Weight-based minimums act as a safety floor:

| Weight category | Approximate weight | Minimum hinges |
|---|---|---|
| Lightweight | < 15 kg (< 33 lb) | 2 |
| Medium | 15–40 kg (33–88 lb) | 3 |
| Heavy | 40–80 kg (88–176 lb) | 4 |
| Very heavy (security) | > 80 kg (> 176 lb) | 5 |

### Screws per Hinge

Each hinge has **2 leaves** (one on the door, one on the frame). Each leaf has 2, 3, or 4 holes depending on the hinge model:

| Hinge type | Holes per leaf | Screws per hinge |
|---|---|---|
| Standard residential (2½″–3″ butt) | 2 | 4 |
| Heavy-duty / ball-bearing (3½″–4″) | 3 | 6 |
| Commercial / security | 4 | 8 |

### Standard Hinge Placement

- **Top hinge**: 7 inches (≈18 cm) from the top of the door.
- **Bottom hinge**: 11 inches (≈28 cm) from the bottom.
- **Middle hinge(s)**: evenly spaced between top and bottom hinges.

### Waste Buffer

Add **10% for precision carpentry** and **15% for rough construction** to cover stripped screw heads, dropped fasteners, and pilot-hole corrections.

## Quick Reference Table

| Door type | Height | Weight | Hinges | Screws (4/hinge) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hollow-core interior | 80″ / 2.03 m | ~20 lb / ~9 kg | 2–3 | 8–12 |
| Solid-core interior | 80″ / 2.03 m | ~60 lb / ~27 kg | 3 | 12 |
| Solid exterior (wood/fiberglass) | 82″ / 2.08 m | ~100 lb / ~45 kg | 4 | 16 |
| Heavy steel / security door | 84″ / 2.13 m | >180 lb / >80 kg | 5 | 20–40 |
| Cabinet / closet door | 60″ / 1.52 m | ~15 lb / ~7 kg | 2 | 8 |

faq.q: How many hinges does a standard interior door need?
faq.a: A standard interior solid-core door (about 2.05 m / 80″ tall, 60–80 lb) needs **3 hinges**. The rule is 1 hinge per 30 inches (≈75 cm) of height: ⌈80/30⌉ = 3. Lightweight hollow-core doors under 60 lb on 2-hinge setups are common in older construction but most modern building codes and trade guidelines recommend 3 hinges for solid-core doors.

faq.q: How many screws go on a standard door hinge?
faq.a: A standard residential butt hinge has **2 holes per leaf × 2 leaves = 4 screws per hinge**. Heavy-duty or ball-bearing hinges (4″ / 100 mm) often have **3 holes per leaf × 2 = 6 screws**. Commercial-grade hinges can use **4 holes per leaf × 2 = 8 screws**. Always fill every hole — omitting screws concentrates load on fewer points and causes premature wear.

faq.q: What size screws should I use for door hinges?
faq.a: For standard residential interior doors: **#8 × 1¼″ flat-head wood screws** (coarse thread). For exterior or solid doors: **#8 × 2" or #10 × 2½"** to reach the structural framing. Security/exterior doors: at least one screw per leaf should be **3" long** to reach the stud behind the casing — this dramatically increases kick-in resistance. Do not use drywall screws; they are brittle and fail under shear loads.

faq.q: Should I add a waste buffer to my screw count?
faq.a: Yes. Industry practice is **10% for precision work, 15% for rough construction**. On a 10-door job you'd add 10–15 extra screws — small cost that prevents a trip back to the hardware store. Common losses: stripped heads in hardwood, dropped fasteners, pilot-hole drift, and screws that split the wood and must be relocated.

faq.q: How many hinges does a heavy exterior door need?
faq.a: Exterior solid-wood or steel doors typically weigh 100–200 lb (45–90 kg) and require **4–5 hinges**. A 2.10 m (83″) door: height rule gives ⌈83/30⌉ = 3, but the weight-based minimum overrides to **4**. For doors over 200 lb (90 kg), use 5 heavy-duty hinges with 3-hole leaves (6 screws each) and 3" structural screws reaching the stud.

faq.q: Where are hinges placed on a door?
faq.a: Standard placement: **top hinge 7" (18 cm) from the top edge**, **bottom hinge 11" (28 cm) from the bottom**, and **middle hinges evenly spaced between**. Example for a 2.05 m (80.7") door with 3 hinges: at 7″, 40.35″, and 69.7" from the top (or equivalently at 69.7", 40.35", and 11" from the bottom). This distribution minimizes stress concentration and door sag.

faq.q: Can I use the same formula for cabinet or closet doors?
faq.a: The height/weight formula works, but cabinet and closet doors typically use **cup hinges (European concealed hinges)** rather than butt hinges. Cup hinges mount with a 35 mm Forstner hole and 2–4 screws per hinge, adjustable in 3 axes. For standard overlay cabinet doors: 2 cup hinges for doors under 60 cm, 3 for doors 60–120 cm. Brands: Blum, Hettich, Salice.

faq.q: How do I calculate hinges for a door that is both tall and wide?
faq.a: For extra-wide doors (over 37–48 inches / 94–122 cm wide), add one extra hinge to the standard height-based count. A wide door moves the center of gravity further from the hinge barrel, increasing the bending moment on the top hinge. For doors wider than 48", consult the hinge manufacturer's load table — the rated capacity per hinge changes significantly with door width.

faq.q: How do I fix a hinge whose screw hole is stripped?
faq.a: Three options in order of severity: (1) **Toothpick-and-glue method** — push wooden toothpicks or matchsticks with wood glue into the hole, let dry 24 h, then re-drive the original screw; (2) **Larger screw** — move up one gauge (#8 → #10) or length (1¼" → 2") to catch fresh wood; (3) **Hinge relocation** — shift the hinge 1" up or down to reach undamaged wood (requires patching and re-mortising the old location).
